title: How Spain Got Rich From a Mistake (and Still Went Broke)
backups: The Spanish Empire: Silver, Gold and Four Bankruptcies
The Empire Where the Sun Never Set, Explained
desc:
For about two centuries one red mountain in Bolivia produced a huge share of all the silver in the world. That silver paid for armies, palaces and wars on three continents and made Spain the empire on which the sun never set. Yet the king who owned it went bankrupt four times.

This is Part 2 of our Spain series. It starts with a sailor who got lost: Columbus, sure he had reached Asia. Then Cortes and the fall of the Aztecs, Pizarro and the room full of gold, the silver mines of Potosi and the coin that became the model for the dollar. Then Philip II, El Escorial, Lepanto and the Armada, a long decline, Napoleon, the wars of independence, and finally 1898, when one explosion in Havana harbour ended a 400-year empire.
chapters: Potosi: the mountain that eats men
sources: John H. Elliott, Imperial Spain 1469-1716 (1963); Henry Kamen, Empire: How Spain Became a World Power (2003); Hugh Thomas, Rivers of Gold (2003); Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003); Kris Lane, Potosi: The Silver City That Changed the World (2019); Geoffrey Parker, The Grand Strategy of Philip II (1998); Mauricio Drelichman and Hans-Joachim Voth, Lending to the Borrower from Hell (2014); Louis A. Perez Jr., The War of 1898 (1998).
note: Population and casualty numbers are historians' estimates. The cause of the USS Maine explosion has never been proven.
